blocks.text: A 52-year-old tells you his wife says he is 'ignoring her', and that he turns his good ear towards the television. A tuning fork and thirty seconds at the bedside will tell you whether the fault lies in the ear's plumbing or in its wiring.

blocks.markdown: **The hearing pathway.** Sound is gathered by the pinna and external canal, converted to vibration by the tympanic membrane, amplified by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) across the middle ear, and transferred to the cochlear fluid at the oval window. The organ of Corti transduces fluid waves into nerve impulses carried by the cochlear nerve to the brainstem and cortex. Failure at the canal, drum or ossicles produces *conductive* loss; failure of the cochlea or the cochlear nerve and beyond produces *sensorineural* loss; both together give *mixed* loss.

blocks.title: Conductive versus sensorineural hearing loss
blocks.text: **Conductive:** sound cannot be transmitted mechanically to the cochlea (wax, middle ear fluid, perforation, ossicular fixation as in otosclerosis, ossicular erosion by cholesteatoma). Bone conduction, which bypasses the middle ear, is intact. **Sensorineural:** damage to the hair cells or nerve (ageing, noise, ototoxic drugs such as gentamicin and cisplatin, Meniere's disease, vestibular schwannoma, congenital causes). Both air and bone conduction are reduced.

blocks.markdown: **Tuning fork tests.** Use a 512 Hz fork, which is struck on the elbow or knee, not on a hard surface. In the **Rinne** test, compare air conduction (fork beside the ear) with bone conduction (base on the mastoid): normally air is louder (Rinne positive). In conductive loss bone conduction is louder (Rinne negative) once the air-bone gap is large enough, roughly 20 dB or more. In sensorineural loss air is still louder than bone, though both are quieter. In the **Weber** test the vibrating fork on the midline forehead is heard centrally in normal ears; it lateralises to the **worse** ear in conductive loss and to the **better** ear in sensorineural loss. A *false-negative Rinne* occurs in a profoundly deaf ear because the fork is heard by the opposite cochlea, so masking is needed. Tuning forks are screening tests; pure tone audiometry quantifies loss.

rows: Away from the affected ear (towards the better ear)
Air thresholds worse than bone: air-bone gap
Air and bone thresholds both raised, no gap
Presbycusis, noise, ototoxic drugs, Meniere's, schwannoma
blocks.caption: Interpreting tuning fork and audiometric patterns

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the forks
blocks.prompt: A 60-year-old man says his left hearing is poor. In the right ear, Rinne is air louder than bone. In the left ear, Rinne is also air louder than bone. Weber is heard in the right ear. Interpret.

steps.text: Rinne is positive on both sides, so neither ear shows a significant conductive deficit.
Weber lateralises to the right. If the left ear had a conductive loss the sound would go to the left; instead it goes to the better right ear.
Therefore the left ear has sensorineural loss (the right cochlea hears the central vibration better).

Next step: audiogram. Unilateral sensorineural loss is investigated for retrocochlear causes (for example vestibular schwannoma) by MRI via ENT, and sudden onset (within about 3 days) is treated as an emergency needing same-day specialist care.

blocks.answer: Left sensorineural hearing loss; confirm by audiometry and look for a retrocochlear cause.

blocks.caption: AC: air conduction; BC: bone conduction; PTA: four-frequency pure tone average (a common convention; some use three frequencies)

blocks.markdown:
**Otitis media.** *Acute otitis media* (AOM) is middle-ear infection, usually following a viral upper respiratory infection that blocks the eustachian tube; it is commonest in young children. Typical organisms are *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. Features: otalgia, fever, irritability, reduced hearing and a red, bulging tympanic membrane; if the drum perforates, pain eases and purulent otorrhoea appears. Most cases settle within days with analgesia and time; antibiotics are considered for systemic illness, high risk or persistence, and choice and dosing follow the BNF and NICE guidance.

*Otitis media with effusion* (glue ear) is a painless middle-ear fluid with conductive hearing loss, a dull retracted or amber drum and often a flat tympanogram; it often resolves, and grommets are considered when hearing loss persists. *Chronic suppurative otitis media* is a persistent discharge through a perforation. **Cholesteatoma** is keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear (often from an attic retraction pocket) causing foul discharge, conductive loss and bone erosion; it needs surgery.

blocks.title: Complications of otitis media
blocks.text: Extracranial: tympanic perforation, hearing loss, **acute mastoiditis** (post-auricular swelling and erythema, protruding pinna, tender mastoid), facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis. Intracranial: meningitis, extradural or brain abscess, lateral sinus thrombosis. Suspect these when a child with otitis media is toxic, has severe headache, neck stiffness, drowsiness or a post-auricular swelling, and arrange emergency admission.

blocks.title: Worked example: an unwell child
blocks.prompt: A 5-year-old has had 2 days of ear pain and fever of 38.9 C, then 3 days later becomes lethargic with a swollen, red area behind the right ear and the pinna pushed forwards and downwards. Identify the problem and management.

steps.text: Initial ear pain with fever suggests AOM; the post-auricular swelling with pinna protrusion indicates spread to the mastoid air cells: acute mastoiditis.
The lethargy raises concern about an intracranial extension (meningitis or abscess).

Management: emergency admission, IV antibiotics per local protocol and BNF, imaging (CT with contrast) to look for subperiosteal or intracranial collections, ENT and paediatric review; surgery (mastoidectomy or drainage) if abscess or failure to improve.

blocks.answer: Acute mastoiditis with possible intracranial complications; urgent admission, IV antibiotics and imaging.

blocks.markdown: **Vertigo** is an illusion of movement, typically spinning. Peripheral causes (inner ear and vestibular nerve) usually give severe vertigo, horizontal or torsional nystagmus that beats away from the lesion, nausea, and no new neurological signs; central causes (brainstem or cerebellar stroke, tumour, demyelination) may show vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, severe unsteadiness, diplopia, dysarthria or limb signs.

rows: Brief (under 1 minute), triggered by head position, such as turning in bed
Dix-Hallpike: torsional upbeat nystagmus with latency, fatigues; treat with canalith repositioning (Epley)
Single severe attack lasting days, with nausea; no recurrent pattern
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve; settles over days to weeks with vestibular rehabilitation
Inner ear inflammation, often viral or complicating otitis media
Episodic attacks lasting from about 20 minutes to hours
Fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
Endolymphatic hydrops; salt reduction and specialist care
Acute, persistent, often with other neurological signs
Direction-changing or vertical nystagmus; use structured bedside tests such as HINTS and image urgently
blocks.caption: Distinguishing common causes of vertigo

points: Rinne and Weber together separate conductive from sensorineural loss; Weber goes to the worse ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in sensorineural loss, and audiometry quantifies the air-bone gap.

Acute otitis media is common in children and usually self-limiting, but mastoiditis and intracranial extension are emergencies; glue ear causes painless conductive loss and cholesteatoma needs surgery.
Vertigo patterns (brief positional, days-long continuous, episodic with fluctuating hearing, or central) point to BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere's disease or a central cause.
Antibiotic choice and doses should be checked against current BNF and NICE guidance.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has noticed gradually worsening hearing in the left ear over three years, with tinnitus; her mother had similar problems. On Rinne testing the left ear hears bone louder than air and the right ear hears air louder than bone. The Weber test is heard louder in the left ear. Otoscopy shows a normal drum. What is the most likely pattern and cause?

options.text: Left conductive loss, such as from otosclerosis

questions.correctOptionText: Left conductive loss, such as from otosclerosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: negative Rinne on the left and Weber to the left, with a normal drum and family history.
distractorRationale.b: Would give a positive Rinne and Weber to the right.
distractorRationale.c: Weber would go to the right and the right Rinne would be negative.
distractorRationale.d: Weber would lateralise to the left but the left Rinne would be positive.

questions.explanation: A negative Rinne on the left shows bone conduction is better than air, and the Weber to the left confirms a conductive loss there. A normal drum with progressive loss and a family history fits ossicular fixation such as otosclerosis; audiometry would show an air-bone gap.

questions.stem: In a patient with unilateral conductive hearing loss, the Weber test is heard louder in the affected ear.
questions.explanation: In conductive loss, background noise masking is reduced in the affected ear, and the bone-conducted sound is heard better there, so the Weber lateralises to the poorer ear. In sensorineural loss it lateralises to the better ear.

questions.stem: Pure tone audiometry in a patient's right ear gives an air conduction threshold of 55 dB HL and a bone conduction threshold of 15 dB HL at 1 kHz. Calculate the air-bone gap in dB.
questions.explanation: The air-bone gap equals the air conduction threshold minus the bone conduction threshold, 55 - 15 = 40 dB. A gap of this size shows a conductive component, such as middle ear fluid or ossicular disease.

questions.stem: A patient's air conduction thresholds are 20, 30, 45 and 55 dB HL at 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz. Using the four-frequency average convention, calculate the pure tone average in dB HL.
questions.explanation: The mean is (20 + 30 + 45 + 55)/4 = 150/4 = 37.5 dB HL. Some services use a three-frequency average, so the convention should always be stated.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has had a high fever and ear pain for two days. Today his temperature is 39.4 C, he is drowsy, vomits, and has neck stiffness. The left tympanic membrane is red and bulging. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Emergency admission for assessment of intracranial complications, with IV antibiotics per protocol
Oral analgesia and review in 48 hours
Grommet insertion as a day case

questions.correctOptionText: Emergency admission for assessment of intracranial complications, with IV antibiotics per protocol

distractorRationale.a: Correct: features suggest meningitis complicating otitis media.
distractorRationale.c: Not the immediate treatment for a toxic child.
distractorRationale.d: Contraindicated and irrelevant in acute infection.

questions.explanation: Drowsiness, vomiting and neck stiffness in a child with otitis media suggest meningitis or other intracranial extension. This is an emergency needing admission, IV antibiotics according to local guidance and urgent imaging or lumbar puncture as appropriate.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old is noted by his teacher not to hear well. He has had no pain or fever. Otoscopy shows a dull, retracted, amber tympanic membrane with an air bubble behind it, and Rinne is negative in both ears. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: painless, afebrile conductive loss with fluid behind an intact drum.
distractorRationale.b: Needs post-auricular swelling, fever and ear pain.
distractorRationale.c: Vertigo, tinnitus and sensorineural loss in adults.
distractorRationale.d: Foul discharge and an attic retraction or perforation.

questions.explanation: Painless conductive loss in a child with a dull, amber drum and fluid is typical of glue ear. It often resolves spontaneously, and grommets are considered when hearing loss persists, as it can affect speech and learning.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has recurrent attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about three hours, each preceded by a feeling of fullness in the right ear and accompanied by low-pitched tinnitus. Audiometry shows a fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
distractorRationale.b: Attacks are seconds and triggered by head position.
distractorRationale.c: A single prolonged attack without hearing loss.
distractorRationale.d: Causes persistent central signs, not recurring episodes with hearing change.

questions.explanation: The classic tetrad is episodic vertigo lasting from tens of minutes to hours, fluctuating sensorineural loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, attributed to endolymphatic hydrops. The history differentiates it from positional or neural causes.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman experiences a brief spinning sensation lasting about 20 seconds whenever she lies down on her left side. Hearing is normal and neurological examination is unremarkable. Which test and treatment are most appropriate?

options.text: Dix-Hallpike test, then a canalith repositioning manoeuvre
Urgent MRI of the internal auditory meati

questions.correctOptionText: Dix-Hallpike test, then a canalith repositioning manoeuvre

distractorRationale.b: For unilateral sensorineural loss, not positional vertigo with normal hearing.

questions.explanation: Brief, positionally triggered vertigo with normal hearing is BPPV from displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal. The Dix-Hallpike test provokes torsional nystagmus, and the Epley manoeuvre repositions the debris.

questions.stem: Describe how you would differentiate BPPV, vestibular neuritis and Meniere's disease on history and examination, and name two features that should make you suspect a central cause.
markingGuide: BPPV: seconds, triggered by head position, normal hearing, Dix-Hallpike torsional nystagmus with latency and fatigue
Vestibular neuritis: single severe attack over days, nausea, no hearing loss, horizontal nystagmus away from lesion, settles over weeks
Meniere's: episodes of 20 minutes to hours, fluctuating sensorineural loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
Central red flags: vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, severe gait unsteadiness, diplopia, dysarthria, limb ataxia, new severe headache
Central suspicion leads to urgent imaging and specialist assessment
questions.explanation: Marks are given for linking each cause to its time course, triggers and hearing change, and for naming at least two central red flags. A good answer states that peripheral nystagmus beats in one direction and suppresses with fixation.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has acute otitis media. Describe the typical presentation and list the main extracranial and intracranial complications.
markingGuide: Otalgia, fever, irritability, reduced hearing, red bulging tympanic membrane; otorrhoea after perforation
Usually follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection; common organisms are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
Extracranial: perforation, hearing loss, acute mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis
Intracranial: meningitis, extradural or brain abscess, lateral sinus thrombosis
Antibiotic decisions follow current NICE and BNF guidance
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes both clinical and otoscopic features and separates local from intracranial complications. The importance is recognising the red flags that need admission.
